text.p: Following are some of the major events to have occurred on July 23 in history:
1757 - Domenico Scarlatti, Italian composer and harpsichordist, died. He composed over 500 keyboard sonatas, using new techniques and achieving brilliant effects.
1759 - Russians under Saltikov defeated the Prussians at Kay, eastern Germany, in the Seven Years' War; 6,000 Prussians were killed.
1785 - King Frederick II of Prussia formed Die Furstenbund (League of Princes) to curb the ambitions in Germany of Emperor Joseph II.
1840 - The Union Act was passed by the British Parliament, uniting Upper and Lower Canada with equal representation for both of the former provinces.
1875 - Isaac Merritt Singer, U.S. inventor, died. He developed the first practical sewing machine in 1851 which was the first to use continuous and curved stitching.
1885 - Ulysses Simpson Grant, commander of the Federal army during the latter part of the U.S. Civil War and U.S. president from 1869-77, died.
1886 - Sir Arthur Whitten Brown, British aviator who with Alcock made the first transatlantic flight in 1919, born.
1888 - Raymond Chandler, U.S. novelist and creator of the Philip Marlowe detective character in "The Big Sleep" and "Farewell My Lovely" and many others, born.
1892 - Haile Selassie, Emperor of Ethiopia from 1930, born. He fled into exile in 1936 after the Italians invaded, returned in 1941 and ruled until he was deposed in 1974.
1916 - Sir William Ramsay, Scottish chemist, Nobel Prize winner and discoverer of helium, argon and other inert gases, died.
1925 - Ketumile Masire, president of Botswana, born; he took power shortly after the death of the country's first president, Sir Seretse Khama, in July 1980.
1930 - Glenn Curtiss, U.S. aviation pioneer whose aircraft were widely used in World War One, died.
1931 - Victor Korchnoi, Russian chess grandmaster who defected to the West, born.
1933 - Sir Richard Rogers, British architect and designer of the Pompidou Centre in Paris and the Lloyd's building in London, born.
1948 - D. W. Griffith, U.S. film producer and director of the silent film epics "Birth of a Nation", and "Intolerance", died.
1951 - Marshal Philippe Petain died in prison. He was French army marshal and head of the collaborating Vichy government in France from 1940-44 and was subsequently sentenced to life in prison.
1952 - An army coup led by General Neguib overthrew and banished King Farouk in Egypt.
1955 - Cordell Hull, U.S. secretary of state 1933-44, died; awarded the 1945 Nobel Peace Prize for his work in organising the United Nations.
1973 - Edward Vernon (Eddie) Rickenbacker, U.S. aviator and ace fighter pilot during World War One, died.
1974 - The Greek armed forces chiefs invited Constantine Karamanlis to return from exile in Paris and form a government.
1974 - Nicos Sampson resigned as president of Cyprus and was replaced by Glafkos Clerides.
1982 - The International Whaling Commission voted for a total ban on commercial whaling to take effect in 1985.
1986 - Prince Andrew married Sarah Ferguson; they became the Duke and Duchess of York.
1989 - Italy's 49th post-war coalition government was sworn in, with Giulio Andreotti as prime minister.
1993 - John Major won a vote of confidence debate in Parliament, clearing the way for British ratification of the Maastricht treaty.
1994 - Soldiers seized power in Gambia after rampaging through Banjul in a dispute over pay. President Sir Dawda Jawara took refuge on a U.S. Navy ship.
1996 - Jessica Mitford, crusading author best known for her indictment of the funeral industry in "The American Way of Death", died.
